messages.subject: Statistical learning and data mining
messages.body_plain:
Short course: Statistical learning and data mining

Trevor Hastie and Robert Tibshirani, Stanford Univ.

Georgetown University Conference Center
Washington, D.C
Sep. 19-20, 2002 

This two-day course gives a detailed overview of statistical
models for data mining, inference and prediction.
With the rapid developments in internet technology, genomics and
other high tech industries, we rely increasingly more on  data analysis
and statistical models to exploit the vast amounts of data
at our fingertips. 

This sequel to our popular Modern Regression and Classification course
covers many new areas of unsupervised learning and data mining,
and  gives an in-depth treatment of some of the hottest tools
in supervised learning.

The first course is not a pre-requisite for this new course.

Day one focusses on state-of-art  methods for supervised
learning including PRIM, boosting and support vector machines.
Day  two covers unsupervised learning including clustering,
principal components, principal curves and  self-organizing maps.
Many applications will be discussed, including DNA expression arrays.
These are one of the hottest new areas in biology!

###################################################
Much of the material is based on the best selling book:

  Elements of Statistical Learning: data mining, inference and prediction 

(Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, Springer -Verlag, 2001).

//http://www-stat.stanford.edu/~tibs/ElemStatLearn/index.html

 A copy of this book will be given to all attendees. 

###################################################

go to the site

http://www-stat.stanford.edu/~hastie/mrc.html

for more information and online registration.

messages.subject_clean: Extracting the Hat matrix from a least-squares fit
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-Plus users

 

 

I have fitted an OLS regression model to data that are 
related as log(y) ~ log(x). However when the conditional means are 
back-transformed to the original scale (ie exponentiated) they are geometric 
means and I require the arithmetic mean (Richard Jarrett discussed this only 
recently). I wish to apply a correction for this estimator proposed by 
El-Shaarawi & Viveros (1997, Environmetrics 8, 569-582).

 

1. The correction involves an operation on the Hat 
matrix. Could someone suggest how I could extract the hat 
matrix for an "lm" object as I have searched the Help and the s-news 
archive without success. 

 

2. The function hat( ) for extracting the diagonal of the Hat matrix uses 
the qr( ) function which I do not understand. Is there are 
straightforward introduction on QR decomposition somewhere?

 

3. I would also like to obtain the similar matrix from 
a Generalized Least Squares model :

    (X' V^-1 X)^-1 X' V^-1.  

 

Any guidance with this problem would be much appreciated!

 

 

 

Hugh Jones

Centre for Natural Resources
NSW

>
> 1. The correction involves an operation on the Hat matrix. Could someone
> suggest how I could extract the hat matrix for an "lm" object as I have

lm.influence(lmfit)$hat

see ?lm.inluence.

>
> 2. The function hat( ) for extracting the diagonal of the Hat matrix
> uses the qr( ) function which I do not understand. Is there are
> straightforward introduction on QR decomposition somewhere?

Yes.  Any good linear algebra or statistical computing book will cover
this.  However, what you need is a text which does linear regression via
the QR decomposition.  Although I've taught it that way for many years
(on and off) I don't know of such a text.

It's difficult to know at what level to start here, perhaps

@Book{Gentle.98,
  author =       {James E. Gentle},
  title =        {Numerical Linear Algebra for Applications in Statistics},
  publisher =    {Springer-Verlag},
  year =         {1998},
  address =      {New York},

}

might be suitable?

> 3. I would also like to obtain the similar matrix from a Generalized
> Least Squares model :
>     (X' V^-1 X)^-1 X' V^-1.

GLS is done by transforming to OLS.  So if you use lm.gls in library MASS
it will be obtained by lm.influence.

messages.subject: Re: Extracting the Hat matrix from a least-squares fit
messages.subject_clean: Extracting the Hat matrix from a least-squares fit
messages.body_plain:
Dear Brian and Hugh,

As I read Hugh's posting, he wants the whole hat matrix, not just the
diagonal. Although it's crude, I suggest using the definitional formula
for the hat matrix, which should work fine if the data set isn't very
large and the model matrix isn't ill-conditioned -- something like the
following:

hat.matrix <- function(model){
    X <- model.matrix(model)
    X %*% solve(crossprod(X)) %*% t(X)
    }

Of course, if this is something that Hugh needs to do often, then
investing the time to learn more about QR decompositions would make sense.

I hope that this helps,
 John

messages.subject: multiple criteria in lme
messages.body_plain:
dear s-plus users,

i have a longitunal outpatient psychotherapy data set on which i
performed a number of linear mixed models so far, e.g.

a.lme <- lme(data = amb.stat, random =  ~IN.THER | CODE, fixed = IMPAIR
~ IN.THER,  na.action = na.omit) ### no covariate

b.lme <- lme(data = amb.stat, random = ~IN.THER | CODE, fixed = IMPAIR ~
WHERE * IN.THER, na.action = na.omit) ## covariate setting

with IN.THER = time in psychotherapy, CODE = patient id, IMPAIR = psych.
impairment, and WHERE = setting (clinic vs. outpatient).

now, we had the idea of modelling different criteria, i.e. change over
time in psychological AND physical impairment over time. when plotting
the mean effects of the models described above, i always plotted time on
the x- and (change of) impairment on the y-axis. the idea is now to
create a three-dimensional space in which change on two outcome criteria
(lateron also effects on change of covariates) over time would be
modelled. in Pinheiro, J. C. & Bates, D. M. (2000). Mixed-effects models
in S and S-PLUS, i couldn't find anything really helpful for tackling
this problem.
any - also speculative - ideas would be highly appreciated.

thanks

bernd

messages.subject: Q on lme and nlme?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, all:

I was doing some analyses using lme and nlme and found out something strange
for the estimated fixed effects:

Let's use model (13.1) (Guide to Statistics Vol 1,Splus 2000):

 d_ij=(beta_0+b_i0)+(beta_1+b_i1)*age_j+epsilon_ij

as the example. 
1. fit model (13.1-above) as:
  Ortho.fit  <- lme(fixed=distance~age, data=Orthodont, random=~age|Subject)
2. I want to force the variance-covariance matrix for the random effect to
be diag, 
   then I fit the model again using:
  Ortho.fit2 <- update(Ortho.fit1, random=pdDiag(~age))
3. If I only assume b_i0 as random effect and fix the b_i1, then I fit the
model using:
 Ortho.fit3 <- lme(fixed=distance~age, data=Orthodont, random=~1|Subject)

The strange thing is that the estimated fixed effects are exactly the same.
I remember that the mle and reml of these parameters are dependent on the
variance-covariance matrix. Am I wrong?

Any comments and suggestions?

Din

messages.subject: Control Mortality in Probit/Logistic Regression
messages.body_plain:
Dear Splus'ers,

When conducting lethality biological assays, we regress the transformed
proportion mortality (probit or logit, sometimes Gompertz, etc.) on the dose
or log(dose).  However, at times mortality sometimes occurs in the control
group.  We assume that the same degree of mortality applies to the remaining
doses.  We can incorporate this control mortality in the likelihood and
solve for the additional parameter.

Has anyone written any Splus code to solve this extended likelihood
function?

Sincerely
Barry Zajdlik

messages.body_plain:
Susan Rasch, Technical Support Engineer at Insightful, was kind enough to 
respond to my inquiry, and explain this behavior.  The problem was fixed in 
Splus 2000 (using one of the '__nn' files to store an otherwise 
DOS-compatible object name of the form 'con.xx', etc), but apparently the 
fix has not yet propagated into Splus 6 for windows.

Susan Rasch wrote:

----------------------------------------------------------------------------

This is a Windows-only problem and generalizes to any object name of the 
form "con.x" and "prn.x", where "x" can be anything.  Windows treats these 
as referring to the DOS console and printer, respectively.

You can see this by going to a DOS console and trying to run, for example,

	notepad con.1

It will fail with an "Access Denied" error (at least on Windows 
2000).  There are a few more odd names that you can't use, like aux.*, 
nul.*, lpt*.*, com*.*, ...

We need to put in some code to work around this.  I have filed a bug report 
on this problem so that it will be fixed for a future release.

Thank you for your help in tracking down this problem in S-PLUS!
----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hello,

I have an array, say "W", arranged like that :

> W
      X1     X2     X3    Y1     Y2    Y3 
1  41893  12803  12803 12202 121847 96500
2 133033 302643 302643 40409 149891 62261

Well, the answer is only this one :

Error in apply(w, 1, wilcox.test(w[, 1:3], w[, 4:6])): "wilcox.test" is not

So, the command is not understood and there is a mistake in using
wilcox.test as such inside  apply() . Is somebody knowing what is wrong with

information.

André MERY

France

--------- David Maxwell wrote ---------

Yves,
    What does .Random.seed now contain? If it is not
in the correct form then call set.seed to reset it.
For example: 

> set.seed(999) 
> .Random.seed
[1] 21 14 49 16 0 1 32 22 36 23 28 3

I hope I have understood your question correctly and
this helps.

David Maxwell. 

--------- Jean-Paul Fox wrote ---------

Hi,
   I do not know how this problem occurs but before
trying it again you should remove .Random.seed within
the work directory by typing rm(.Random.seed).

   It is possible that after removing the random drawn
numbers it will work.

   Good luck,

   Jean-Paul Fox. 

--------- Brian D. Ripley wrote ---------

Start S-PLUS

rm(.Random.seed)
runif(1)
q()

   Next time you start up, this should be fine.

   .Random.seed is an S object, and it has got
corrupted. That should give you a new copy unless your
.Data directory is really messed up (when you would
need to move it to a safe place and start again). 

--------- Chuck Taylor wrote ---------

Yves,
   The problem has nothing to do with importing Excel.
The problem is that .Random.seed has somehow been
corrupted. You can fix this by simply deleting it:

  remove(".Random.seed")

  Please let bugs at insightful.com know if you find a
way to reliably reproduce this problem.

messages.subject: Re: strange quirk in Splus 6/Win2000
messages.body_plain:
> OK, can someone explain this conspiracy?  I got the same 
> thing with Splus 6.0 on NT, but not on Linux.

S-PLUS on Windows uses files to store objects, but in Windows some file names 
are illegal (e.g. PRN, LPT1, and many more).  Such object names get mapped to 
file names like __1 by S-PLUS.  S-PLUS does handle objects named "con" and 
"con." in this way, but it turns out any "con.???" is illegal in Windows (don't 
ask me why!) and we missed those.  It'll be fixed in a subsequent release.  In 
the meantime, the only workaround on Windows is to use an object name which 
does not match the con.??? pattern.

The problem doesn't occur on Linux because Linux (like most Unix-a-likes) has a 
real filesystem which allows any filename.

# David Smith

messages.subject: Re: strange quirk in Splus 6/Win2000
messages.body_plain:
As explained by this link,
http://www.oreilly.com/catalog/jpower/bugfixes/
Windows 95/98/NT reserves filenames con.* and nul.* for it's own use.

I had a similar problem when I tried to install a PERL distribution one time
that had a filename of "con.pl" in the directory tree.  The install failed.

I suppose the nearest UNIX equivalent might be if you tried to actually
create a file by the name of "." or "/dev/nul".  UNIX might be smart enough
to handle this, but common sense says you shouldn't do it.

Kevin Wright

messages.subject: polygon question summary
messages.body_plain:
below is the list of 7 very useful replies I got to my previous question

> does anybody have an Splus function that can check, whether a point is

> inside a polygon (not necessarily a convex one)?

Thanks very much to everybody who replied.

Ing. Marek Brabec, PhD

1. dr. Robert M. Key wrote:
In the older versions of SpatialStats there is a function called
"points.in.poly" which did what you want. I think that this may
be included in the general release of newer versions of S. If not,
the listing is:

function(x, y, polygon)
{
        nx <- length(x)
        if(length(y) != nx)
                stop("x and y should be the same length\n")
        if(!is.list(polygon))
                stop("\"polygon\" must be a list! \n")
        if(any(is.na(charmatch(c("x", "y"),
as.character(names(polygon))))))
                stop("\"polygon\" must have components \"x\" and
\"y\"!\n")
        points.in <- logical(nx)
        for(i in 1:nx)
                points.in[i] <- pip(x[i], y[i], polygon)
        points.in

2. dr. Sundar Dorai-Raj wrote:
Look at the splancs library:

library(splancs)
set.seed(102)
poly <- data.frame(x=c(-.5,.5,.5,-.5,0),y=c(-.5,-.5,.5,.5,0))
points <- data.frame(x=runif(20,-1,1),y=runif(20,-1,1))

in.poly <- match(pip(points,poly),points)

plot(x=0,y=0,xlim=c(-1,1),ylim=c(-1,1),xlab="x",ylab="y")
polygon(poly,density=F,lwd=3,col=6)
points(x=points$x[ in.poly],y=points$y[ in.poly],col=2)
points(x=points$x[-in.poly],y=points$y[-in.poly],col=4,pch=15)

If you have splus 6 for Windows, you can download splancs from either

http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/MASS3/Winlibs/

Other versions may be found from

http://www.maths.lancs.ac.uk/~rowlings/Splancs/

In the future, it's always nice if you give your email a more
descriptive subject (e.g. "Points in Polygon") and also tell the list
what version of Splus you are using. To do the latter, type version at
the command line in Splus. For example, on my computer I get:

> version
Professional Edition Version 6.0.3 Release 2 for Microsoft Windows :
2001

3. dr. Rolf Turner wrote:
The functions enclosed below should do what you want.  They are
extracted from the ``spatstat'' package for R, written by Adrian
Baddeley (of the University of Western Australia) and myself.  This
package is available from CRAN.  We are hoping to produce a version
of the package for Splus, fairly soon, but this hasn't happened
yet.

The first function, inside.xypolygon(), does the real work.  It calls
the second function, verify.xypolygon(), to do some consistency
checking.

The arguments ``pts'' and ``polly'' given to inside.xypolygon() must
be ***lists***, each with components ``x'' and ``y'', of equal length
(within each list).

Example:

> xx <- c(0.79,0.73,0.65,0.43,0.51,0.09,0.51,0.49,0.72,0.78,0.64,0.83)
> yy <- c(0.75,1.00,0.89,0.87,0.56,0.48,0.38,0.26,0.29,0.39,0.60,0.71)
> x <- runif(100)
> y <- runif(100)
> plot(x,y,xlab='',ylab='',xlim=c(0,1),ylim=c(0,1))
> polygon(xx,yy,density=0)
> a <- list(x=x,y=y)
> b <- list(x=xx,y=yy)
> iii <- inside.xypolygon(a,b)
> points(x[iii==1],y[iii==1],pch='o')

Hope this helps.
inside.xypolygon <- function (pts, polly, test01 = TRUE)
{
    verify.xypolygon(pts)
    verify.xypolygon(polly)
    x <- pts$x
    y <- pts$y
    xp <- polly$x
    yp <- polly$y
    npts <- length(x)
    nedges <- length(xp)
    score <- rep(0, npts)
    on.boundary <- rep(FALSE, npts)
    for (i in 1:nedges) {
        x0 <- xp[i]
        y0 <- yp[i]
        x1 <- if (i == nedges)
            xp[1]
        else xp[i + 1]
        y1 <- if (i == nedges)
            yp[1]
        else yp[i + 1]
        dx <- x1 - x0
        dy <- y1 - y0
        if (dx < 0) {
            xcriterion <- (x - x0) * (x - x1)
            consider <- (xcriterion <= 0)
            if (any(consider)) {
                ycriterion <- y[consider] * dx - x[consider] *
                  dy + (x0 * dy - y0 * dx)
                contrib <- (ycriterion >= 0) *
ifelse(xcriterion[consider] ==
                  0, 1/2, 1)
                score[consider] <- score[consider] + contrib
                on.boundary[consider] <- on.boundary[consider] |
                  (ycriterion == 0)
            }
        }
        else if (dx > 0) {
            xcriterion <- (x - x0) * (x - x1)
            consider <- (xcriterion <= 0)
            if (any(consider)) {
                ycriterion <- y[consider] * dx - x[consider] *
                  dy + (x0 * dy - y0 * dx)
                contrib <- (ycriterion < 0) *
ifelse(xcriterion[consider] ==
                  0, 1/2, 1)
                score[consider] <- score[consider] - contrib
                on.boundary[consider] <- on.boundary[consider] |
                  (ycriterion == 0)
            }
        }
        else {
            consider <- (x == x0)
            if (any(consider)) {
                yconsider <- y[consider]
                ycriterion <- (yconsider - y0) * (yconsider -
                  y1)
                on.boundary[consider] <- on.boundary[consider] |
                  (ycriterion <= 0)
            }
        }
    }
    score[on.boundary] <- 1
    if (test01) {
        if (!all((score == 0) | (score == 1)))
            warning("internal error: some scores are not equal to 0 or
1")
    }
    attr(score, "on.boundary") <- on.boundary
    return(score)
}

verify.xypolygon <- function (p, fatal = TRUE)
{
    whinge <- NULL
    if (!is.list(p) || length(p) != 2 || length(names(p)) !=
        2 || any(sort(names(p)) != c("x", "y")))
        whinge <- "polygon must be a list with two components x and y"
    else if (is.null(p$x) || is.null(p$y) || !is.numeric(p$x) ||
        !is.numeric(p$y))
        whinge <- "components x and y must be numeric vectors"
    else if (length(p$x) != length(p$y))
        whinge <- "lengths of x and y vectors unequal"
    ok <- is.null(whinge)
    if (!ok && fatal)
        stop(whinge)
    return(ok)
}

4. dr. Taylor Z. Todd wrote:
I got this some years ago, either off this mailing list or
by private email from Mr. Perkins (can't remember).
inside.polygon <- function(test, vertices) {

   # Author:  Peter Perkins <peter at caliban.ucsd.edu>
   # Modified by Z. Todd Taylor...

   # determine whether test points are inside a simply closed polygon.
   # this routine uses EUCLIDEAN geometry, not SPHERICAL.
   #
   # test:         matrix (or 2-vector) of test points
   # vertices:     matrix of polygon vertices, last vertex same as first

   #
   # col1 = x-coords, col2 = y-coords
   #

   n <- nrow(vertices) - 1
   if(!is.matrix(test)) test <- matrix(test, nrow = 1, byrow = T)

   # translate to coords centered at each test point
   x <-  - outer(test[, 1], vertices[1:n, 1], "-")
   y <-  - outer(test[, 2], vertices[1:n, 2], "-") #

   # tan(theta) = (v1 x v2) / (v1 * v2)
   i2 <- c(2:n, 1)
   theta <- atan(x * y[, i2] - y * x[, i2], x * x[, i2] + y * y[, i2])

   # sum angles about each test point
   theta <- abs(theta %*% rep(1, n))
   ifelse(abs(theta - 2 * pi) < 1e-06, T, F)
}

5. dr. Tim Hesterberg wrote:
Below are a couple of versions of a function that does this.
These are some very old work (before I started working at
MathSoft/Insightful);
my notes indicate that InPolygon2 has been more extensively tested,
while InPolygon3 should be faster, but is buggy; so take at it only if
InPolygon2 is too slow.

Tim Hesterberg

InRange _ function(x, a, b){
  if(length(a) == 2.) {
    b <- a[2.]
    a <- a[1.]
  }
  else if(length(a) * length(b) != 1.)
    stop("a and b must have length 1 in InRange, or a may have length
2")

InPolygon2 _ function(px,py,x,y){
  # px and py are vertices of a polygon (in order around the edge)
  # x & y are vectors, which are the coordinates of points
  n _ length(x)

  #Quick check, which points might possibly be in  the polygon?
  which1 _ InRange( x, min(px), max(px)) & InRange( y, min(py), max(py))

  if(!any(which1)) return( rep(F,n))
  xw _ x[which1]
  yw _ y[which1]
  which2 _ (InRange( xw+yw, min( px+py), max(px+py)) &
            InRange( xw-yw, min( px-py), max(px-py)))
  xw _ xw[which2]
  yw _ yw[which2]
  if(!any(which2)) return( rep(F,n))
  which3 _ which1; which3[ which1 ] _ which2
  ##which1 & which3 have the same length as the original x & y

  #Now check which of those points are actually in the polygon
  px2 _ c( px[-1], px[1] )  #End of polygon segments
  py2 _ c( py[-1], py[1] )
  slopes _ (py2-py)/(px2-px)
  intercepts _ py2 - slopes * px2
  bad _ is.na(intercepts) | (intercepts==Inf) | (intercepts== -Inf)
  slopes _ slopes[!bad]
  intercepts _ intercepts[!bad]

  m _ length(xw)
  #Rows will be points in the following matrix operation, columns are
lines
  # Count number of lines which are above each point
  above _ RowSums( ((yw - outer(xw,slopes)) <= rep2(intercepts,m))
                    & (( outer(xw,px[!bad],"<=")
                        + outer(xw,px2[!bad],"<=") == 1)) )
  which4 _ which3; which4[ which3 ] _ (above %% 2 == 1)
  which4
}

region.inside <- function(test, vertices)
{
# determine whether test points are inside a simply closed polygon.
# this routine uses EUCLIDEAN geometry, not SPHERICAL.
#
# test:         matrix (or 2-vector) of test points
# vertices:     matrix of polygon vertices, last vertex same as first
#
# col1 = x-coords, col2 = y-coords
#
        n <- nrow(vertices) - 1
        if(!is.matrix(test)) test <- matrix(test, nrow = 1, byrow = T)  #
# translate to coords centered at each test point
        x <-  - outer(test[, 1], vertices[1:n, 1], "-")
        y <-  - outer(test[, 2], vertices[1:n, 2], "-") #
#
# tan(theta) = (v1 x v2) / (v1 * v2)
        i2 <- c(2:n, 1)
        theta <- atan(x * y[, i2] - y * x[, i2], x * x[, i2] + y * y[, i2])  
   #
#
# sum angles about each test point
        theta <- abs(theta %*% rep(1, n))
        ifelse(abs(theta - 2 * pi) < 1e-06, T, F)
}

I couldn't resist a try at something a little more general.
The idea is that if you go in any direction, say due north,
and count boundary crossings, an odd count means your in, and even
means you are out, assuming the region is defined by closed curves
(here connect-the-dots loops).  Concave is ok.  Islands and holes
are ok.  Assuming the data are in a list of n_i by 2 matrices, each
with the first point replicated at the end (so a call to lines() draws
a closed loop), then this seems to work:

  is.north <- function(b,x) approx(b[c(1,3)],b[c(2,4)],x[1])$y>x[2]
  crossings <- function(b,x){
    pairs <- cbind(b[-nrow(b),],b[-1,])
    dimnames(pairs)[[2]] <- c("x1","y1","x2","y2")
    maybe <- pairs[ (pairs[,1] <  x[1] & pairs[,3] >= x[1])|
                    (pairs[,1] >= x[1] & pairs[,3] <  x[1]),,drop=F]
    if (length(maybe) == 0) result <- 0
    else result <- sum(apply(maybe,1,is.north,x))
    result
  }
  inside <- function(x,bound) 
    as.logical(sum(sapply(bound,crossings,x))%%2)

First get pairs of points.  Then collect the pairs (in maybe) whose x
coordinates straddle the test point (x).  Then use approx to test if the
candidate segments are to the north.  Here's an example of use:

# Draw boundaries on a 100 by 100 field via mouse:
plot(c(0,100),c(0,100),type="n")
get.points <- function(n){
   points <- sapply(locator(n),round) # enter via mouse
   rbind(points,points[1,]) # Copy first point to end.
}
points1 <- get.points(20)
lines(points1)
points2 <- get.points(10)
lines(points2)
points3 <- get.points(10)
lines(points3)
points <- list(points1,points2,points3)

# Now we have an interesting boundary.  Test a point:
inside(unlist(locator(1)),points)

Kristi,

Here's a pair of functions I wrote a while back to do the job. I presume the 
code is quite
efficient, because it is incomprehensibly dense. It uses the 
"count-the-crossings" approach. NB that the result is not well-defined for 
points on the edge; it may come out either T or F. 

The function 'in.poly' is the main one. The parameter "xy" should be a
data.frame or 2-column matrix of x and y coordinates. "poly" can either be:

(1) a n-vertex polygon in the same format with n rows (last row does not need to
equal first row as this is done automatically).

(2) the result of a previous call to 'poly.for.testing' with the original
polygon as input.

In other words, the following are equivalent:

> points_ data.frame( x=c(0,1), y=c( 0, 1.5))
> polypoints_ data.frame( x=c( 0.5, 2, 2), y=c( 0, 0, 6))
> in.poly( points, polypoints)
[1] F T
> temp.poly_ poly.for.testing( polypoints)
> in.poly( points, polypoints)
[1] F T

The result is, as you see, a logical vector with one element per point.

If you are repeatedly testing lots of points for inclusion within the same
polygon, and you're doing it within a loop rather than with one call to
"in.poly", it is much more efficient to call 'poly.for.testing' first.

Here's the code-- good luck

in.poly_ function( xy, poly)
{
  if( ncol( poly)==2)
    poly_ poly.for.testing( poly)
  n_ nrow( xy); np_ nrow( poly); nnp_ rep( n,np)
  check1_ xor( xy[,1]>=rep( poly[,1], nnp), xy[,1]>rep( poly[,3], nnp))
  check2_ rep( poly[,2], nnp) + rep( poly[,4], nnp) * xy[,1] > xy[,2]
  as.vector( matrix( check1 & check2, n, np) %*% rep.int( 1, np) %% 2 > 0)
}
poly.for.testing_ function( xy)
{
  if( is.list( xy))
    xy_ as.data.frame(xy)
  if( !is.matrix( xy) || ncol( xy)!=2 || !is.numeric( xy[,1]) || 
      !is.numeric( xy[,2]))
stop( "xy must by nX2 numeric matrix or data.frame")

# Columns of poly are start.x, a, end.x, b
  xy_ as.matrix( xy)
  poly_ matrix( c( xy, xy[ c( 2:nrow( xy), 1), ]), ncol=4)
  poly_ poly[ poly[,1] != poly[,3], ]
  poly[,4]_ (poly[,4]-poly[,2])/(poly[,3]-poly[,1])
  poly[,2]_ poly[,2] - poly[,1]*poly[,4]
  poly
}

First, thanks go to Robert Garret for providing the history of this
topic on S-news; to Brian Ripley for outlining an efficient algorithm;
to Peter Perkins for his program "region.in" (which was the first
mentioned in
Garret's history); to John Wallace for providing a copy of the same
under the title "region.inside"; and to Franz Mueter, for pointing to the 
"points.in.poly" function, which is part of the Spatial module,
and is written directly in C.

Peter Perkins program, given below, is based on centering the extreme
points around each test point and checking if the sum of radians from the
test
point to successive extreme points is close to 2*pi.

Brian Ripley's suggestion:

 A convex polygon is defined by r enclosing half-planes a + bx + cy >= 0.
So find them (you need the extreme points in order, which I think chull
gives, then the lines pass through successive pairs) and make a matrix A
with columns a b c. The test is then 

((cbind(1, X) %*% t(A) < 0) %*% rep(1, r)) == 0

which gives a vector with T for inside, F for outside.

 This seems like a good idea, so I implemented a version of it. I was
too lazy to check which side of each half-plane the hull was was on,
so I just computed the average m of the extreme points (which is 
guaranteed to be inside the region) and checked that each test point
was on the same side of all the boundary lines as m. This function
"Inside" is given below, right after "region.in".

 As far as efficiency, I sampled 10,000 points at random from the unit
square and tested if they were in the convex quadrilateral defined by
> hull
     [,1] [,2] 
[1,]  0.0  0.0
[2,]  0.2  0.4
[3,]  0.6  1.0
[4,]  1.0  0.0

The two procedures worked about equally well:

> unix.time(region.in(testpts,rbind(hull,c(0,0))))
[1] 2.3399963 0.1100001 5.0000000 0.0000000 0.0000000
> unix.time(Inside(testpts,hull))
[1] 2.18999481 0.03000021 3.00000000 0.00000000 0.00000000

Both were much faster than my initial crude attempt:
>unix.time(apply(testpts,1,inside,h=hull))
[1] 167.30   0.77 343.00   0.00   0.00
where 
inside _ function(pt,hull) min(chull(rbind(pt,h)))>1

Thanks to all for your patience and information --

region.in <- function(test, vertices)
{
# determine whether test points are inside a simply closed polygon.
# this routine uses EUCLIDEAN geometry, not SPHERICAL.
#
# test:         matrix (or 2-vector) of test points
# vertices:     matrix of polygon vertices, last vertex same as first
#
# col1 = x-coords, col2 = y-coords
#
       n <- nrow(vertices) - 1
       if(!is.matrix(test)) test <- matrix(test, nrow = 1, byrow = T)  #
#
# translate to coords centered at each test point
       x <-  - outer(test[, 1], vertices[1:n, 1], "-")
       y <-  - outer(test[, 2], vertices[1:n, 2], "-") #
#
# tan(theta) = (v1 x v2) / (v1 * v2)
       i2 <- c(2:n, 1)
       theta <- atan(x * y[, i2] - y * x[, i2], x * x[, i2] + y * y[,
i2])     #
#
# sum angles about each test point
       theta <- abs(theta %*% rep(1, n))
       ifelse(abs(theta - 2 * pi) < 1e-06, T, F)
}

____________________________________________________________
                
Inside _ function(pts,h=hull){
#
# Input:
#    pts -- (n x 2) matrix of test points
#      h -- ([k+1] x 2) matrix of (ordered) vertices,
#                 [with last row = first row]
# Output:
#     (n x 1) logical vector indicating inclusion of tests points
#           in the convex polygon formed by h 
#
n _ nrow(pts)
k _ nrow(h)-1
if (!all(h[1,]==h[k+1,])) {
    h_ rbind(h,h[1,])
    k _ k+1}
#
# compute slopes and intercepts of boundary lines
#
b _ diff(h[,2])/diff(h[,1])
a _ diag(h[1:k,] %*%t(cbind(-b,1)))
#
#   compute centroid and its residuals from boundary lines
#
m _ rep(1/k,k) %*%  h[1:k,]
r0 _  m[2] - (a + b* m[1])
#
#  compute residuals of test points from boundary lines
#
r _ outer(pts[,2],rep(1,k)) - outer(pts[,1],b) - outer(rep(1,n),a)
signs _ (r %*% diag(r0)) > 0
ans _  as.vector(signs %*% rep(1,k) == k)
ans}

> din't work. I think that this has something to do with
> S scope rules. (SPLUS 2000 Professional for Windows)
> 

Yes. It is a consequence of the scope rules. To make it work
                lis[[i]] <- lapply(1:10, function(k,i) x[i] + rnorm(1), i=i)
or, to emphasize the difference between formal and actual arguments,
                lis[[i]] <- lapply(1:10, function(k,z) x[z] + rnorm(1), z=i)

Inside the anonymous function, S will look for i in the current frame, then
frame 1, frame 0, and, if it still doesn't find it, S will look in the
search path starting with the current database. So if 'i' exists in the
current directory, S will use that one, which is probably not what you want
and may be hard to catch if it doesn't lead to an error. This sometimes
happens to me when I build up the body of a function by testing things in
the session frame first and then forget to pass some of the inputs through
the argument list.

I would like to thank Bill Venables, Nick Ellis,
Dennis J. Murphy, Patrick Burns, Brad Mann, Renaud
Lancelot and Gabriel Baud-Bovy, for their useful
replies.

The answer to my problem was to use the following:

f <- function(x){
        n <- length(x)
        lis <- vector(length = n, mode = "list")
        for(i in 1:n) {
                lis[[i]] <- lapply(1:10, function(x,z)
                x[z] + rnorm(1), z=i)
        }
        unlist(lis)
}

Thank you everyone for your replies. I created the following function with
example based on some of your advice:

## x = matrix to draw image plot of
## middle =  value to define as the middle color
image.sym <- function(x, middle){
     image(x)
     t <- round(abs((max(mat)-middle)/(middle - min(mat))))
     guiModify("GraphSheet", Name = "GSD2",
          ImageColorTable = "255,0,0|0,0,0|0,255,0",
          NumImageColors = "3",
           NumImageShades = paste("49", as.character(t*49), sep = ",") )
}

mat <- matrix(c(seq(-2,0,length = 50), seq(0,4,length = 50))  , nrow = 10)
image.sym(mat,0)

The result of this example creates an image plot where -2 is all green the
value of 0 is black and 4 is completely red.
The above function could be modified to take in other colors than red,
black, and green and could even be explanded to create multiple convergence
points for colors.  The only problem I have with this function is that it
modifies the whole graphsheet.  If I used the par statement to show, for
example, 4 image plots with different middle points this function would not
work.  Maybe someone out there could fill in this gap.

messages.subject: Summary of responses: Extracting the Hat matrix from aleast-squares fit
messages.subject_clean: Summary of responses: Extracting the Hat matrix from aleast-squares fit
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-Plus users

 

Thanks to Brian Ripley, Bill Venables, John Fox, Thomas 
Yee and Stephen Smith for responding to my query. This was just what I 
needed. Their replies are summarised below.

 

 

Bill suggested 
using                     
X <- model.matrix(lmObject) to obtain the design 
matrix

 

John Fox suggested the following which worked well for me as my X matrix 
was simple (only one regressor):

 

Although it's crude, I suggest using the definitional formula for the hat 
matrix, which should work fine if the data set isn't very large and the model 
matrix isn't ill-conditioned -- something like the following:

hat.matrix 
<- function(model){
    X <- 
model.matrix(model)
    X %*% solve(crossprod(X)) %*% 
t(X)
    }

>From Bill Venables: 

 

The QR decomposition is merely a convenient way of finding an 
orthonormal basis for the model subspace.  You do it in two 
steps.

 

    myQR <- 
qr(X)            
                # 
does the main work

    Q <- 
qr.Q(myQR)          
              # will get you the 
orthonormal basis as a matrix

    h <- (Q * 
Q) %*% rep(1, ncol(Q))  # will get you the diagonal of the hat 
matrix

 

 

Thomas Yee's comments answered an unvoiced concern of 
mine:

 

Just a comment on when the X is ill-conditioned. 
Rather 
than forming the cross product t(X) %*% X explicitly,
one should use the 
QR-decomposition to form t(R) %*% R instead, where
X = Q %*% R (provided the 
QR method is used in the first place; it is so
with lm). Then invert t(R) %*% 
R.  This is done in summary.lm(). 

Here's a simple example with help 
from the R manuals. 

    hilbert <- function(n) { i 
<- 1:n; 1 / outer(i - 1, i, "+") }
    n = 
9
    p = 6
    X <- 
hilbert(n)[,1:p]

    fit = lm(rnorm(n) ~ X - 
1)

    hat1 = X %*% summary(fit)$cov.unscaled %*% 
t(X)     # More numerically stable

    hat2 = X %*% solve(crossprod(X)) %*% 
t(X)              
   # Fails on most machines 

If hat2 doesn't fail, then 
increasing n and p soon will.
The blue and white book has some details about 
this, and also any book on
numerical linear algebra with reference to least 
squares problems.

 

 

On doing something similar for a generalized least squares 
model, (X' V^-1 X)^-1 X' V^-1. 

Bill Venables suggested:

 

[WNV]  This is not a 
hat matrix, of course.  The obvious way might be the 
quickest

 

    VX <- 
solve(V, X)

    Mat <- 
solve(crossprod(X, VX), t(VX))

 

If V is diagonal you can do 
some of the work by declaring it as a weights vector, 
&c.

 

Prof. 
Ripley:

 

GLS is done by transforming to OLS.  So 
if you use lm.gls in library MASS
it will be obtained by 
lm.influence.

 

Prof. Ripley on a straightforward introduction on QR 
decomposition :

 

Yes.  Any good linear algebra or statistical computing book will 
cover
this.  However, what you need is a text which does linear 
regression via
the QR decomposition.  Although I've taught it that way 
for many years
(on and off) I don't know of such a text.

It's 
difficult to know at what level to start here, perhaps

James E. Gentle, 
1998.  Numerical Linear Algebra for Applications in 
Statistics,
          
Springer-Verlag, New York  ISBN = 0-387-98542-5

might 
be suitable?

On the correct back-transformation when 
assuming a lognormal regression model:

>From Stephen Smith :

 

D. Bradu and Y. Mundlak 1970 Estimation in log-normal linear 
models, Journal of the 

         American 
Statistical Association 65, 198--211

A fisheries application is 
given in:

Stratis Gavaris,1980 Use of a multiplicative model to estimate 
catch rate and

        effort from 
commercial data, Canadian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic 
Science 37,

        
2272--2275

Bill Venables referred to Finney's work based on the 
Rao-Blackwell theorem. I think that the reference is 

Finney DJ 1941. On the distribution of a variate whose 
logarithm is normally distributed. 

      J. Roy. Stat. Soc. B, 7, 
155-161 

 

 

My original question:

I have fitted an OLS regression model to data that are 
related as log(y) ~ log(x). However when the conditional means are 
back-transformed to the original scale (ie exponentiated) they are geometric 
means and I require the arithmetic mean (Richard Jarrett discussed this only 
recently). I wish to apply a correction for this estimator proposed by

messages.subject: Re: QUERY: Categorizing data
messages.body_plain:
For your 1st question, see the help page for cut.

For your second question:  Why do you need to "fit a normal distribution" to
find mean and sd?  Let's say your vector is named "x", then x.mean <-
mean(x) and x.sd <- sqrt(var(x)) gives you the mean and sd.  You can then
use something like my.cutpts <- x.mean + seq(-3, 3)*x.sd as the cut points.

How are you going to assess the "fit"?

Andy

messages.subject: summary.lme
messages.body_plain:
In regard to my question about summary.lme, Dr. José Pinheiro provided
the following response:

The summary.lme function now includes an argument "correlation" which is
used to control the printing of the fixed-effects correlations. The
default value is FALSE, but of course you can use

> summary(object, corr = T)

to get the correlations printed. The previous behavior was to always
include the correlations, which, depending on the number of fixed
effects in your model, could lead to fairly large output.

Respectfully, 
Frank R. Lawrence

messages.subject: Progress: Converting S-Plus C++ v6 to C++ .NET
messages.subject_clean: Progress: Converting S-Plus C++ v6 to C++ .NET
messages.body_plain:
Greetings All:

 

Several days ago I reported difficulty using Visual Studio
with S-Plus 6.1, even though S-Plus by all accounts works well with C++
v6.  It appears that while C++ v7 (i.e. C++ .NET) is very much like its
predecessor, S-Plus 6.1 doesn’t recognize it as such. 
(Re-installing S-Plus 6.1 does not recognize Visual Studio v7.)

 

Andy Liaw suggested I ask the Insightful folks directly,
which I did.  I was disappointed in the result, however, since they
provided detailed instructions (below) for doing things in C++ v6, but I don't
have v6.  I have v7; v6 is no longer available.  Insightful further reported
that they don’t have v7 yet.  (They were very nice, however.)

 

I was able to get the pointers pointing to the appropriated
directories and files, and so am reporting my progress to date, as was
requested by several list members.

 

NOTE: I’m using Windows XP Professional.  My
installation of S-Plus is C:\Program Files\Insightful\splus61.  If yours
is different please make the appropriate path changes.  My project files
are in C:\Documents and Settings\ ... \My Documents\Visual Studio Projects

 

C++ v6 details (from Insightful):

...............................................................

The default setup for Visual Studio C++ .NET does not
include the S-Plus goodies which must be pointed to manually.  In C++ v6
this was done this way, according to the Insightful people:

 

1. From 'Tools' menu, select 'Options...'

2. Select 'Directories' tab of the 'Options' dialog

3. Select 'Include files' from 'Show directories for'
drop-down list 

4. Add to the 'Directories:' list-box, two directories:
'SHOME\include' and

   'SHOME\sconnect', where SHOME is the actual
directory that S-PLUS installed in    the local machine

5. Select 'Library files' for 'Show directories for'
drop-down list 6. Add to 'Directories:' list-box, the directory to SHOME\lib

 

For each project that builds a DLL linked to the S-PLUS
engine,  you need to specify the import libraries:

 

1. From the 'Project' menu, select 'Settings'

2. Select 'Link' tab of the 'Settings' dialog

3. Replace the contents in the 'Output file name' edit-box
by'S.dll' 

4. Select 'General' for 'Category' in the drop-down list 

5. Add to the 'Object/library modules' edit-box: 'sqpe.lib sconnect.lib'

...............................................................

 

Visual Studio C++ .NET (My progress to date.)

Unfortunately v7 (Visual Studio C++ .NET) doesn't have these
menus and tabs.  I was however able to divine the mechanism for pointing
to the appropriate libraries.  I am using the gausssdl.cxx example
provided with S-Plus 6.1 rather than writing my own code at this learning
stage.  While I was able to point to the appropriate libraries, I ran into
a compiler error that stopped me dead.  The offending line in the
offending file, line 18 of c:\Program Files\Insightful\splus61\sconnect\spchar.h(18):
fatal error C1001: INTERNAL COMPILER ERROR (compiler file 'msc1.cpp', line
2844)

has me baffled, however since that line contains only a left
bracket: {

 

In any event I seem to have overcome one large hurdle, viz.
telling Visual Studio C++ .NET where to find the S-Plus resources.  Here
is what to do:

 

1.  Open the C:\Program
Files\Insightful\splus61\samples\GaussSDL folder and clicked on gausssdl.cxx to
open the Visual Studio and begin with the gausssdl.cxx file.

2.  Click on the "gausssdl" icon in the
Solution Explorer window (upper right window).

3.  Now click on the View menu and choose Properties.

3.a   Click on the C/C++ folder, and notice the
"Additional Include Directories" line at the top.

3.b   Place a semicolon at the end of the line
containing the current list and paste in C:\Program
Files\Insightful\splus61\include

3.c   Add another semicolon and paste in
C:\Program Files\Insightful\splus61\sconnect

4. Click on Apply

5. Now open the Linker folder (still within the gausssdl
Property Pages).

5.a   On the Additional libraries Directories
line, add a semicolon and paste C:\Program Files\Insightful\splus61\lib

5.b   Add another semicolon and paste C:\Program
Files\Insightful\splus61\sconnect

5.c  The Output File should already be set to S.dll by
having opened the gausssdl.css file.

5.d  Click Apply, then OK.

 

You're now ready to build the solution. Well, you should be
ready but since I get a fatal error, I've obviously stumbled over something.

 

Click the Build menu, then Build Solution, and you'll get everything
lined up and off to the races only to bomb on line 18 of the spchar.h file

 

That's my progress to date.  If anyone can go further
please tell me the secret.

 

Thanks.

 

Charles Annis, P.E.

Charles.Annis at StatisticalEngineering.com

phone:
561-352-9699

eFAX: 503-217-5849

http://www.StatisticalEngineering.com

messages.subject: Progress report: Using C++ .NET with S-Plus 6.1
messages.subject_clean: Progress report: Using C++ .NET with S-Plus 6.1
messages.body_plain:
Fellow s-news Listers:

I recently reported difficulty using the latest version of MS C++ (v7,
a.k.a C++ .NET) with S-Plus 6.1, which purportedly works well with C++
v6 but C++ v6 is no longer available.

Andy Liaw suggested I ask the Insightful folks directly, which I did.  I
was disappointed in the result, however, since they provided detailed
instructions for doing things in C++ v6, but I don't have v6.  I have
v7; v6 is no longer available.  Insightful further reported that they
don't have v7 yet.  (They were very nice, however.)

The purpose of this note is twofold:  1) To report a method for linking
with the appropriate S-Plus libraries and files that does work with C++
.NET, since other list members have asked for such information, and 2)
to report that spchar.h produces a fatal compiler error in C++ v7, viz.:

c:\Program Files\Insightful\splus61\sconnect\spchar.h(18): fatal error
C1001: INTERNAL COMPILER ERROR (compiler file 'msc1.cpp', line 2844) 

Since spchar.h appears to be the Connect/C++ file, this is a serious
problem.

NOTE: I'm using Windows XP Professional.  My installation of S-Plus is
C:\Program Files\Insightful\splus61.  If your path is different, please
make the appropriate changes to my stuff, below.  My project files are
in C:\Documents and Settings\ ... \My Documents\Visual Studio Projects.
I am using the gausssdl.cxx example provided with S-Plus 6.1 rather than
writing my own code, so I will know any problem is not with my
code-writing. 

Here is how to get C++ .NET to find the S-Plus 6.1 libraries and files.
>>>>>>>>>>>
1.  Open the C:\Program Files\Insightful\splus61\samples\GaussSDL folder
and click on gausssdl.cxx to open the Visual Studio and begin with the
gausssdl.cxx file. 2.  Click on the "gausssdl" icon in the Solution
Explorer window (upper right window). 3.  Now click on the View menu and
choose Properties.
3.a   Click on the C/C++ folder, and notice the "Additional Include
Directories" line at the top.
3.b   Place a semicolon at the end of the line containing the current
list and paste in C:\Program Files\Insightful\splus61\include
3.c   Add another semicolon and paste in C:\Program
Files\Insightful\splus61\sconnect
4. Click on Apply
5. Now open the Linker folder (still within the gausssdl Property
Pages).
5.a   On the Additional libraries Directories line, add a semicolon and
paste C:\Program Files\Insightful\splus61\lib
5.b   Add another semicolon and paste C:\Program
Files\Insightful\splus61\sconnect
5.c  The Output File should already be set to S.dll by having opened the
gausssdl.css file. 5.d  Click Apply, then OK.

You now should be ready to build the solution, however the compiler
balks at spchar.h
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>

(I tried to post a longer version of this note to the s-news but it
bounced.)

I have again spoken with Insightful (they really are nice folks) and
they're trying to get C++ .NET in-house so they can find a fix for
spchar.h that will work with C++ v7.

Charles Annis, P.E.

eFAX: 503-217-5849
http://www.StatisticalEngineering.com

the files to their original lower case names (in Windows Explorer) they
were immediately accessible.

messages.subject: Re: guiOpenView
messages.body_plain:
It is probably (almost surely, in fact) a visibility problem on the search
path.  Many functions are designed to work effectively at the command level
and do not translate easily into functions where the search path is slightly
obscure.

Inside your function instead of

        PesticideDataFrame <- CHEMlist[["Pesticide"]]

try putting

        assign("PesticideDataFrame", CHEMlist[["Pesticide"]], frame = 1)

and see what happens.  This is a fairly standard dodge to cater for these
situations, but not one that should be used routinely.  There are dangers
associated with it in some situations.

Bill Venables.

messages.subject: Re: Tree regression puzzlement
messages.body_plain:
David Parkhurst asks:

>  -----Original Message-----
> From:         David Parkhurst [mailto:parkhurs at indiana.edu] 
> Sent: Monday, July 15, 2002 11:30 AM
> To:   s-news at lists.biostat.wustl.edu
> Subject:      [S] Tree regression puzzlement
> 
> I have a dataframe containing a response y and several explanatory x's.
> If I run
> pairs(), it is clear that y is fairly strongly correlated with at least a
> couple
> of the x's.  N=16 rows.
> 
> If I then run rpart(y~.), that returns only a single node---it doesn't  do
> even a
> single split. 
         [WNV]  The problem is that you only have 16 observations.  The
default rpart control is for minsplit to be 20.  Unless a node has at least
minsplit observations a split will not be attempted.  You can change this
but there are some good reasons for it being set so high.  the ordinary
tree() function has a much more liberal approach.

        Also you should remember that correlations are measures of linear
association and tree models are highly nonlinear.  Unexpected things can
happen with tree models when ordinary linear models are much more suitable.

        With just 16 observations, though, I would not expect any modelling
approach to show very much.  You may be asking quite a lot of a very small
amount of data, especially if you have an appreciable amount of residual
variation to contend with.

>    That seems odd to me.  Is there some logical way that could occur,
> or does that result indicate I am doing something wrong?
> 
> Thanks for any insight.
> 
> Dave Parkhurst

For an n x n matrix, how could I vectorize the calculation of all the pairwise differences among the matrix elements such that the resulting symmetric matrix would then be n^2 x n^2?  For example, if the matrix is 3 x 3, the resulting matrix would be 9 x 9 and contain the elements xi - xj for all pairs of i,j.

messages.subject: Re: Vectorizing the calculation of pairwise differences
messages.subject_clean: Vectorizing the calculation of pairwise differences
messages.body_plain:
Let 
X be the matrix.  Then the matrix of all pairwise differences of elements 
is

 

A 
<- outer(as.vector(X), as.vector(X), "-")

 

This is an n^2 x n^2 matrix but it is not symmetric - in fact 
it's skew-symmetric: A = -t(A).  

In 
particular the diagonal is zero.

 

Bill Venables.

messages.subject_clean: fitting a polynominal using lm - explicit or using poly
messages.body_plain:
On Mon, 15 Jul 2002, Andrew Czarn wrote:

> to anyone who can assist
>
> i have observed that when i fit a polynominal using lm, i get different
> answers whether i use the form:
>
> lm(outcome~(iv+iv^2)) as opposed to
>
> lm(outcome~(poly(iv,2))
>

Both.

> the splus manual talks about the later being orthogonal, but i
> am still not clear which yields the (more) correct equation.

Both are correct: they are parametrized differently.  poly(iv, 2) expands
in orthogonal polynomials, and iv + I(iv^2) in powers.

Orthogonal polynomials are usually used for numerical stability: it's
not often that this is necessary for a quadratic.

> take this result and know that it was a column subsetting not a row one?
> Does anyone have an answer to how to compensate for this within the
> setMethod call?  I know you could define the function within the setMethod
> to take arguements i and j but that would not be ideal for we want to keep
> the same functionArgNames structure.
> 
> Thanks
> Josh

This doesn't actually relate to method questions directly, but to the
behavior of list(), which drops elements coresponding to missing
arguments.  There are several ways to get around the problem, such as
the following non-obvious, but simple method (assuming you would be
happy with the expressions for the rows & columns rather than the values
of those expressions).

Define
 listWithEmpties <- function(...){ tmp <- substitute(TMP(...));
as.list(tmp)[-1]}

Then:

S+> listWithEmpties(1:2, 3:4)
[[1]]:
1:2

[[2]]:
3:4

S+> listWithEmpties(1:2, )
[[1]]:
1:2

[[2]]:

S+> listWithEmpties(,3:4)
[[1]]:

[[2]]:
3:4

(Be careful, though, the "empty" cells have class "missing"; don't try
to evaluate them directly:

S+> sapply(listWithEmpties(,3:4), "class")
[1] "missing" "call"   
)

On the methods front, perhaps a future "standard" for the S language
will modify the API to make the i,j subscript arguments explicit:

"[" <- function(x, i, j,  ..., drop = T) standardGeneric("[")

The change makes it possible to have methods depending on the class of
the subset arguments.  It's true that this makes matrices and other
two-dimensional arrays a bit more special in the language than they are
now, but in practice they do dominate applications.

messages.subject: Re: Tree regression puzzlement
messages.body_plain:
On Mon, 15 Jul 2002, Aldi Kraja wrote:

> Hi Bill,
> I do not see what is the reason you call the default setting of minsplit
> =20 for RPART "so high"?
> It translates to a minbucket ~ 7. In regression trees for example, this
> means if we want to fit some simple regression line in a leaf, we will
> have available about 7 points.

But that's not what a regression tree does: it fits a constant at a leaf.

> I do think that 7 points can represent
> quite easy a noisy model. You recommend a much more liberal approach? In
> my work I use minsplit=150 and still I am not content sometimes with the
> tree results I see. So what could be the liberal approach in using tree
> package?

tree() uses a minsplit of 10 and a mincut of 5, not so much more
liberal.  But the point is that these are just a limit on tree growth and
trees are meant to be pruned, so generally they only save time (and
problems with exceeding the maximum tree depth of 31).

> Regards,
> Aldi

OBJECTIVE 

With the growth of the Internet and developments in imaging technology,
very large digital image archives have been created and used in numerous
applications. Together with the increase in the number of pictorial 
archives, demands are also growing for methodologies and techniques to
store and retrieve pictorial entities from large image archives. It is
known that colour provides powerful information for data analysis, 
recognition and visualization. As a consequence, colour has become a center 
of interest as a powerful tool in content-based image retrieval, opening
many new directions of research and technology. 

TOPICS 

In this special issue, we focus on the use of colour in the exploration of 
image data repositories for the purpose of content-based image access. As 
long as the primary focus is on colour, the special issue will include
the following topics: 

+ Colour feature extraction 
+ Colour image filtering 
+ Colour image segmentation 
+ Colour models and spaces 
+ Colour-texture models 
+ Combining colour and shape information 
+ Colour invariance and colour constancy 
+ Chromatic adaptation 
+ Handling shadows and illumination 
+ Physics-based matching 
+ Perceptual-based indexing and retrieval 
+ Compression of colour image content 
+ Colour image indexing 
+ Colour image classification 
+ Colour-based feature selection

messages.subject: Re: Tree regression puzzlement
messages.body_plain:
Hi ,

In Bill's and Brian's  text: "MASS", Springer Verlag (there are some editions
now), in the chapter about Tree-based Methods, it is shown in a nice way
the use of pruning back principle. This has a reason: if we have a large
dataset and we grow a tree (in RPART) with a cp as close to zero, for sure
many splits are not necessary (statistical sense of the model fit). In the
technical report of Atkinson and Therneau (That comes together with the RPART
package) it is shown that one can control the growing of a tree based on
minsplit or minbucket settings (?minsplit, ?minbucket) and also on the cp
value (?control; ?rpart.control). Also they have shown that the tree is controlled
also internally based on the model improvement expressed graphically in R^2
(?rsq.rpart). In the discussed case it is the reverse of large sample size.
Sample size is 16. One can look at the data and separate them by hand. If
one wants to convince himself that the separation was on statistical basis,
one can use RPART or TREE. Brian just gave the TREE deafults. In RPART, one
can force the split, by chaning cp to for example 0.0001, which sometimes
cannot happen. The problem all the time is: does the forced split make any
statistical sense? The statistical sense of the regression trees is very
interesting problem and one can find some very useful suggestions if one
does a search in Splus archieves on bagging or boosting.

http://www.biostat.wustl.edu/cgi-bin/search_s-news.cgi

Not a simple question to answer!  What version of S-PLUS, what platform
and what graphics device?  (There are lots of possible answers depending
on the combinations of these, including `not possible'.)

The only reasonably general solution of which I am aware is for the
postscript() device (on Unix, and S+6.x on Windows), using Alan
Zaslavsky's postscriptfonts package (on Statlib, and in a
simpler-to-install form at

http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/S/S+6/postscriptfonts.tar.gz
http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/MASS3/Winlibs/postscriptfonts.zip

).

For italics, font=3 is usually italic, but you would need to use
repeated calls to mtext and trial-and-error to do what you want, whereas
postscriptfonts can do it by embedding escape sequences.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Raquel,

> Raquel Leyva wrote:
> 
> Dear list members,
> I have a file with dates (m,d,y) that I need to convert to Julian
> dates.  I have been successful converting individual dates using the
> command:
> 
> "apr22<-julian(4,22,1997, origin=c(1,1,1997)"
> 
> However, I do not want to convert individual dates but the entire file
> which contains dates from April-July.  My file has the following
> format:
> DATE
> 3/21/1997
> 4/9/1997
> 4/20/1997
> 5/3/1997
> 5/3/1997
> 6/12/1997
> So, the question is how do I transform all my data at once?  Thank you
> for your help.
> 

julian() will take vectors, so the problem lies in parsing your dates.
Here's one solution:

> tmp <- c("3/21/1997","4/9/1997","4/20/1997",
+          "5/3/1997","5/3/1997","6/12/1997")
> tmp.dates <- dates(tmp,format="m/d/y")
> m <- match(as.vector(months(tmp.dates)),month.abb)
> d <- as.vector(days(tmp.dates),mode="numeric")
> y <- as.vector(years(tmp.dates),mode="numeric")
> julian(m,d,y,origin=c(1,1,1997))
[1]  79  98 109 122 122 162
> 

Note that the dates have to be numeric. Since months() returns "Jan",
"Feb", etc. the match() call converts months to 1, 2, etc.

Tested in splus6r2 and splus2000 on win2000pro.

Regards,

messages.subject: Still goodness-of-fit
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to many people for giving me an answer to the following question I
posted last Wednesday :

"I am wondering whether it is possible to easily test the goodness-of-fit of
a distribution curve against a normal distribution curve. For example, I
have a set of data, say X, and using qqnorm(X) and qqline(X) gives me a
graph where points lie almost on the line. So, I am proned to say that the
distribution of X is normal. But I didn't find how to test that easily and
get some p-value showing the reality of the fit. Are there any options that
could be passed to qqnorm in order to test the goodness-of-fit or, if not,
does anybody know the simplest way to do so ? "

But I must acknowledge I am puzzled by the function  ks.gof. The  S+ "Help"
gives the code to use :

ks.gof(x, y = NULL, alternative = "two.sided", distribution = "normal", ...)

and then says that :

"Usually, you must supply the parameters of the hypothesized distribution.
The only exceptions are parameters for the normal and exponential
distributions." 

>From that, I understand that the mean and standard deviation of the data
could be passed to  ks.gof  in the place of the "...", but that is not
necessary if  distribution = "normal".

So, let's take  u <- rnorm(1000)

1°) Using  ks.gof(u, distribution="normal")  gives me a calculated p-value
of 0.241, which is set to 0.5 (I don't understand why but can accept that).
The output specifies also :

alternative hypothesis: True cdf is not the normal distn. with estimated
parameters 
sample estimates:
   mean of x standard deviation of x 
 -0.01145772                 1.04149

>From the previous output, I understand that the sample estimates were used
to test the normality of "u". Then, I supply these parameters to  ks.gof
(which is not necessary according to the "Help"), and I expect to have the
same result.

2°) Using  ks.gof(u, distribution="normal", mean=mean(u), sd=sqrt(var(u)))
gives me now a p-value of 0.6813

Looking at the differences between the 2 p-values, I then thought that the
normal distribution used in  ks.gof  when  "mean ="  and  "sd ="  are not
specified could be N(0,1). Well :

3°) Using  ks.gof(u, distribution="normal" mean=0, sd=1)  gives now me a
p-value of 0.1948..., meaning that my thought was wrong.

Now, the real question is : for assessing whether or not given data follow a
normal law, what is the proper code to use, the 1°) or the 2°) ? Maybe there
is something obvious I missed ? Sorry if this question appears a bit "basic"
to some of you.

Best regards,

André MERY
Aventis  Pharmaceuticals France
Andre.mery at aventis.com

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have come the next couple of days with strange results of the gls function. I think I can summarize what I think I have understood under the following hypothesis:

The argument "singular.ok=T" in the "control" argument does not work if argument "weights" is also specified to gls.

Examples: where Xd.dense and clust.dense produce a singular model.matrix

test_gls(model = tempo ~ Xd.dense + as.factor(clust.dense), control = list(singular.ok = T))

works fine, and ignores the "NA" parameters - as e.g. does glm. Note that anova(test) however cannot estimate anything on the second argument, incorporating NA values, contrary to anova.glm.

testb_gls(model = tempo ~ Xd.dense + as.factor(clust.dense), control = list(singular.ok = T),weights=varConstPower(form=~abs(fitted(.)),fixed=list(const=0.01)),verbose=T)

does not work. More precisely, it gives:

Iteration: 1

Objective: 3166.66349630788 , ms iterations: 3 

varStruct  parameters:

               power 

 0.00519758679260397

Convergence:

 beta varStruct 

    1        NA

There were 36 warnings (use warnings() to see them)

Problem in gls: Missing value where logical needed: if(max(aConv) <= tolerance) {

        break

This also happens if argument weights is completely specified - e.g. by fixing also power. This also happens on other models, with completely different data.

So my questions are:

Is my hypothesis right? Have I missed something? Is there a solution to remedy this?

Thanks very much in advance.

Friendly,

messages.subject: variances for minimization with penalty function?
messages.subject_clean: variances for minimization with penalty function?
messages.body_plain:
Dear s-news readers,

I wish to fit a model using an objective function that is the residual sum
of squares (RSS) plus a penalty function. i.e.

RSS + k * sum [y = 2 to Y] ( f_y / f_y-1 ) **2

where k is fixed and f_y an estimated parameter.

(The penalty function is to stop the differences between some of the
parameters being too large.)

I also want variance estimates for the parameters.

I can use nlminb to do the minimization as all the parameters should be
greater than zero. If the penalty function was not included I could convert
the objective function to the relevant piece of the log-likelihood (assuming
normally distributed errors):  (n/2)*log(RSS/n)
then use nlminb, followed by vcov.nlminb from Venables and Ripley's MASS
library. Correct?

Is using vcov.nlminb still appropriate if I include the penalty function ? 

If not, I would appreciate suggestions on how to estimate parameter
variances for a penalised log likelihood or penalised sum of squares.

Windows 95.
Professional Edition Version 6.0.3 Release 2 for Microsoft Windows : 2001 
MASS library for Venables & Ripley (1999) version 6.2

(For those with an interest in fisheries science the question was triggered
by Cook (1997). Ices J. Marine Science, 54: 924-933)

Thanks for your time,
David Maxwell.

Centre for Environment, Fisheries & Aquaculture Science.

roc.AB.mod.mat <- model.matrix(formula(roc.AB.GJtariff.160702), data = roc.AB)

messages.subject: quantile regression question
messages.body_plain:
I am just starting to use S/R, converting over from SAS.  I want to estimate
the upper quartile in a scatterplot of demographic rates against rainfall in
a small mammal population.  The data looks like this:

|
|*                  * <- point in question
|*
|*  *
|*  *
|*  *   *
|*  *   *   *   *   *
|_______________________________________

Based on a paper by Scharf et al. in Ecology (vol 79, p448) I am trying to
use the qreg package in R to estimate the upper quartile in the data.  My
problem is that I have relatively few data points (~40) which are mostly
distributed at the low end of the x axis, and an outlier in the y direction
at the high end of the x axis.

I would like to find a way either by iteratively weighting the observations
or by bootstrapping the regression to quantify the relationship in the mass
of the data.  I looked in the manual for qreg, and while it allows for
weights, there is no guidance for routines to calculate them.  I also
checked the help archives and on the web, and while I found a bit on the
web, I didnt see much that was specific to my problem.  It seems like this
would be a general issue when working with naturally occurring phenomena
(like rainfall) as there will often be few data points at the extremes.

Any suggestions would be most welcome.

Thanks,

Chris

messages.subject: Re: Problem choosing random-effects variance-covariance struc
messages.body_plain:
The 
example given in the book fits a random intercept for both Sex and age.  
That is done by making 

 

random=age|Subject

 

You 
ask about fitting an AR(1) structure for the residual errors within 
Subject.  To do this, you add

 

corr=corAR1(form=~age|Group).

 

See 
the help for lme, then look at the bottom for corClasses, and then 
corAR1.

 

The 
full call is:

 

Ortho.fit1<-lme(distance~age*Sex, data="" 
random=age|Subject, corr=corAR1(form=~age|Group))

 

See if 
this works.

 

Larry 
Hunsicker

messages.subject_clean: Starting values for random effects, etc, in lme
messages.body_plain:
Hi, folks:

I have been trying to do an lme analysis of a moderately large data set
(1,715 patients with 11 measurement times).  For various reasons I need to
stipulate an unstructured correlation matrix, which obviously adds 55 extra
parameters that the model has to estimate over what would happen with the
assumption of i.i.d. normal errors.  I was not surprised that the model
didn't converge within the default number of iterations.

> date()
[1] "Mon Jul 15 20:49:43 CDT 2002"
> acr9.lme <- lme(l2acr ~ TRT * DAY, data = acr1, random =  ~ 1 | pid,
        corr = corSymm(form =  ~ VisitNo | pid))
> date()
[1] "Mon Jul 15 23:56:50 CDT 2002"
> summary(acr9.lme)
Linear mixed-effects model fit by REML
 Data: acr1 
       AIC      BIC   logLik 
  30898.41 31561.04 -15359.2
.....
Warning messages:
  ITERATION LIMIT REACHED WITHOUT OTHER CONVERGENCE in: ms( ~  -
logLik(lmeSt, lmePars), start = list(lmePars =
        c(coef(lmeSt))), control = list(rel.tolerance = controlvals$ ....

So I reran the model, starting the estimate of the correlation matrix with
the final values of the prior run.  

> date()
[1] "Fri Jul 19 12:24:06 CDT 2002"
> acr11.lme <- lme(l2acr ~ TRT * DAY, data = acr1, random =  ~ 1 | pid,
        corr = corSymm(value = coef(acr9.lme$modelStruct$corStruct, FALSE
        ), form =  ~ VisitNo | pid))
> date()
[1] "Fri Jul 19 16:30:25 CDT 2002"
> summary(acr11.lme)
Linear mixed-effects model fit by REML
 Data: acr1 
       AIC      BIC    logLik 
  30898.06 31560.69 -15359.03
.........
Warning messages:
  ITERATION LIMIT REACHED WITHOUT OTHER CONVERGENCE in: ms( ~  -
logLik(lmeSt, lmePars), start = list(lmePars =
        c(coef(lmeSt))), control = list(rel.tolerance = controlvals$ ....

As you can see, it still didn't converge, though the system must be close to
a convergence since the change in logLik was minimal (0.17).

I have a series of questions resulting from this experience:

1)  Is it possible to include initial estimates for values other than for
the corStruct and varStruct -- such as for the fixed and random effects?
Will using these other close to convergence starting values help this
analysis to converge more quickly?

2)  Pinheiro's book suggests that lme extracts initial parameter estimates
from lm.list, and apparently update also extracts initial estimates from
prior runs of lme.  Which values does it use, and how does it feed these
into the new lme run?

3)  Any suggestions about why the model isn't converging?  I would love to
be able to see the msVerbose=TRUE reports of the iterations, as it might
help me see whether there is an alternation in the logLik values or
something like that.  But as I have previously reported, I can't get
msVerbose to work when I have specified either a corStruct or a varStruct.

Many thanks for any suggestions.

Larry Hunsicker

messages.body_plain:
One of my current projects involves testing k>=2 subpopulation variances and
deciding
if they are equal.  Based on my research, it appears that the
Brown-Forscythe (JASA 
vol. 69, p. 364-367), O'Brien (JASA vol. 74, p. 877-880), and Conover &
Johnson's 
modification (Technometrics vol. 23, p. 351-361) of the Fligner-Killeen
statistic (JASA
vol. 71, p. 210-213) are the three most recommended.  A benefit to these
tests is that
they appear to allow testing of k=2 variances once the omnibus null
hypothesis has been
rejected (using, say, the Bonferroni inequality to adjust for significance
levels).

Two questions:
(1) Does anyone have anything to add to these choices?
(2) Has anyone implemented a package for Splus that performs one or more of
these
tests?

Much appreciation in advance,

 David Paul, Ph.D.

messages.subject: summary statistics for k-nearest neighbors
messages.body_plain:
I would like to calculate summary statistics for a given point in
n-dimensional space based on the k-nearest neighbors of that point.

As a simple example, let's say I have six points in two-dimensional space
(defined by x and y) that take on the values 1-6 (defined by z) and I want
to calculate an average z-value at nine points along a regularly spaced
grid (defined by grid) based on the two-nearest neighbors.

x <- c(1.1, 3.7, 1.5, 3.5, 1.3, 2.8)
y <- c(1.6, 1.9, 1, 1.2, 3.5, 2.7)
z <- 1:6
grid <- expand.grid(x=1:3, y=1:3)

I might create a function, knnsumry(), to do this for me based on a
training set, a test set, the observed values of the test set, the number
of neighbors, and a summary function.

mean.2nn <- knnsumry(train=cbind(x, y), test=grid, z, k=2, function=mean)

And in this example, the output value would be:

mean.2nn
[1] 2.0 2.0 3.0 2.0 4.5 4.0 3.0 5.5 4.0

See also the plot created by the commands below:
plot(x, y, type="n")
text(x, y, z)
points(grid, pch=16)
text(grid$x+0.1, grid$y+0.1, mean.2nn, csi=0.3)

When the function of interest is the mean or the median, you might argue
that some kind of smoother could do the job for me.  But, if the summary
function is more complicated than that, say the variance of the k-nearest
neighbors, then it's not clear to me how a smoother could be used.

Is there an S-PLUS function that carries out this kind of operation?  Or,
alternatively, is there an S-PLUS function that can output a index list
identifying the k-nearest neighbors for a given point?
Thanks in advance for your help.

I'm using S-PLUS 6.0 Professional release 2 on Windows NT.

JVA

messages.subject_clean: Summary: summary statistics for k-nearest neighbors
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to David Paul for his helpful reply.
I came up with the following function which meets my needs.
See original posting below.

JVA

knnsumry <- function(train, test, z, k=2, FUN=mean) {
    ntrain <- dim(train)[1]
    ntest <- dim(test)[1]
    results <- numeric(ntest)
    for(i in 1:ntest) {
        dif <- train - test[rep(i, ntrain), ]
        dst <- sqrt(apply(dif^2, 1, sum))
        results[i] <- FUN(z[dst <= sort(dst)[k]])
        }
    results
    }

For the 2x2 case, I have a script that might help:

fisher <- function(x,a=x[1,1],b=x[1,2],c=x[2,1],d=x[2,2]) {
  #       a | b
  #  x = -------
  #       c | d
  N <- sum(x)
  p <- dhyper(a,a+b,c+d,a+c)
  x <- seq(max(0,a+b-(N-a-c)),min(a+b,a+c))
  phyp <- dhyper(x,a+b,c+d,a+c)
  sum(phyp[phyp<p])+p
}

messages.subject: Parametric survival curves for delayed entry data
messages.subject_clean: Parametric survival curves for delayed entry data
messages.body_plain:
I am currently trying to plot the survival curve for parametric models
for weibull,lognormal and loglogistic distributions using delayed entry
data.

To fit these models, I use censorReg with the appropriate parameters
for delayed entry data. However, there is no function that I can find
that will plot the survival curve for parametric models using censorReg.
So I just take the form of the survivor function for the parametric model
that I am using, plug in the the appropriately transformed parameters
and I should have the survival curve. However, when I plot the survival
curve against a nonparametric estimate of the survival curve, my
parametric survival curve isn't similar to the nonparametric estimate
even though diagnostic plots done beforehand indicate that the parametric
model should provide a good fit to the data. Do I have to somehow correct
for delayed entry in the parametric survival curve estimate? I should
note that when I fit Weibull or exponential models to data of this type,
the survival curve has the same shape as the non-parametric curve but is
just shifted. This doesn't hold when lognormal models are fitted.

Any help would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks,
Denise

I have a nonlinear regression problem similar to the Puromycin 
example of Bate and Watts (1988) Nonlinear Regression Analysis

fm1 <- nls(rate ~ Vm * conc/(K + conc), data = Puromycin,
           subset = state == "treated",
           start = c(Vm = 200, K = 0.05), trace = TRUE)

messages.subject: eps files and enscript
messages.body_plain:
We are using Splus 6.1.2 and GNU enscript 1.6.1 on Solaris 2.6.

In Splus 6.0 we used to create plots as encapsulated postscript files
and embed them in text using enscript.  But the postscript driver has
changed with version 6.1.2 and now this is no longer working.

That is, what we do is
  * generate plots as encapsulated postscript files, one plot per
    file,
  * create a text file with enscript escape codes in the places where
    we want the plots to appear,
  * run enscript on this text file to create an ordinary postscript
    file describing a document with text and plots intermixed.

The enscapsulated postscript plot files appear to be correct---at
least we can view them---and enscript does not complain when we use it
to merge the text and graphics into the ordinary postscript file.  But
the resulting postscript file does not print properly.  On our
printers we get content up to but not including the first plot, and
when viewed under ghostview we get as far as the first plot and then
no more.  The message that ghostview gives is

  Error: /undefined in pos

Below I have included the source for a function that exhibits the
problem.  If you run it in Splus 6.1.2 as

  > plotInEnscript('/tmp/a.ps')

you will get a problem file "/tmp/a.ps."

Thanks for any suggestions.

-----------------------------------------------------------------
epsPlot <-
  function(plotFile = paste(getenv('HOME'),
             'S5/library/enscript/p.ps', sep = '/'))
{
  postscript(file       = plotFile,
             onefile    = F,
             print.it   = F,
             width      = 5,
             height     = 5,
             horizontal = F)
  on.exit(dev.off())
  plot(runif(200),
       main = "Main",
       xlab = "the x lab",
       ylab = "the y lab")
}

plotInEnscript <-
  function(filename = paste(getenv('HOME'),
             'S5/library/enscript/plotInEnscript.ps',
             sep = '/'))
{
  ## Create plot.
  plotFile <- tempfile('plotFile')
  on.exit(unlink(plotFile))
  epsPlot(plotFile)

  ## Create text.
  textFile <- tempfile('enscriptFile')
  on.exit(unlink(textFile))
  writeLines(text = c('first line of text',
                      'second line of text',
                      'here is a plot:',
                      paste('\001epsf{', plotFile, '}', sep = ''),
                      'there it was',
                      'final line of text'),
             textFile)

  ## Enscript the text and plot.
  shell(paste('enscript -e001 -o', filename, textFile),
        output = F)
}
-----------------------------------------------------------------

--

PHZ Capital Partners    508.653.1745 (fax)

Wayland, MA 01778

messages.subject: : Summary of responses to recent questions
messages.subject_clean: : Summary of responses to recent questions
messages.body_plain:
Hello, all,

Yesterday I posted three questions to the list. I'll take the
liberty of summarizing the answers to all three here.

1) I asked why I couldn't import a comma-delimited file, instead
receiving a bizarre error message about .Random.seed. Some people
apparently thought they were too important to be bothered with this
question; for those people I suggest the liberal use of the delete
button in your mail reader, surely the best time-management aid
ever invented. Most respondents, however, actually provided a helpful
response, namely to delete .Random.seed and let S-Plus regenerate
it. I tried this, and it works. No one, unfortunately, was able to
explain what .Random.seed has to do with file import functions, so
that must remain a mystery for now.

2) I asked why I couldn't organize data objects in Object Explorer into
folders, as the documentation suggests I should be able to do. This
question generated a variety of responses. Steven Wofsy
[wofsy at fas.harvard.edu]
suggested that such a problem could arise because of a privilege
mismatch in Windows 2000; that's not the case for me, because I run
S-Plus under the same username under which I installed it. Glenn Treacy
[Glenn.Treacy at ilim.com] suggested using multiple databases, but warns of
the possibility of dealing with corrupted databases. David L Lorenz
[lorenz at usgs.gov] provided a more complete explanation of the procedure
hinted at in the documentation; I haven't tried this yet, but plan to.
Anthony Westerling [leroy at ucsd.edu] suggests using multiple _Data
directories at different positions on the SearchPath, then using objcopy()
and rm() to manage files, and a .first function that attaches the paths
in the correct order. This sounds interesting, but a bit cumbersome; still,
I may try this. John Fennick [jhf at metrocast.net] suggests using multiple
projects, and provides a script for moving data objects between projects.
I'm going to give this a try later today.

3) I asked if anyone knew whether S-Plus for ArcView would work with current
ESRI software. Eran Bellin [ebellin at optonline.net] said "When esri
first released the new version of their product, I called Insightful and
was told that they had no intention of creating a link to the new esri
product.  Perhaps, there is enough interest to change that decision."
Dr. M.Sawada [msawada at uottawa.ca] pointed out that ArcGIS is based on
a completely different data object structure than older versions, and
suggested looking at R (www.r-project.org) and RArcInfo, spdep, etc.
I'm planning to follow that suggestion later today.
